question: What does a route of transmission describe?

options.A: The path a germ takes from a source to a new host
options.B: The specific medication used to kill a virus
options.C: The time it takes for symptoms to show up
options.D: The physical strength of a bacterial cell wall

explanation: The route of transmission is simply the way an infectious agent moves from its reservoir to reach a susceptible person. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T6#GNS313_U1_T6_h1)

question: Why is identifying the route of transmission critical for nurses?

options.A: It guides the choice of proper infection control precautions
options.B: It proves which family member originally brought the illness
options.C: It dictates the required laboratory staining technique
options.D: It determines the exact financial cost of patient care

explanation: When nurses know how a germ travels, they can select the correct barriers like masks, gowns, or handwashing protocols to block it. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T6#GNS313_U1_T6_h1)

question: Which component of the chain of infection is an infected human wound considered?
explanation: An open wound serves as a portal of exit because it is a pathway for pathogens to leave the reservoir body. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T6#GNS313_U1_T6_h2)

question: What happens to the spread of disease if a nurse successfully breaks even one link in the chain of infection?

options.A: The pathogen automatically changes into a harmless bacteria
options.B: The patient develops instant immunity against all other germs
options.C: The infection cycle is stopped and disease spread is prevented
options.D: The reservoir completely disappears from the environment

explanation: Because the chain requires every single link to function, breaking just one link halts the entire transmission process. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T6#GNS313_U1_T6_h2)

question: What defines direct contact transmission?

options.A: Carrying of pathogens by biting insects like mosquitoes
options.B: Inhalation of tiny dried respiratory droplets floating in the air
options.C: Spread of germs through contaminated drinking water supplies
options.D: Physical transfer of pathogens between an infected person and a susceptible host

explanation: Direct contact requires physical touch or direct exposure to bodily fluids without any intermediary objects or surfaces. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T6#GNS313_U1_T6_h3)

question: A patient is admitted with a skin infection spread by direct touch. Which nursing action is most important?

options.A: Placing the patient in a negative pressure isolation room
options.B: Putting on gloves and a gown before touching the patient's skin
options.C: Spraying the hallway air with strong chemical disinfectants
options.D: Boiling all eating utensils before the patient uses them

explanation: Because direct contact involves skin-to-skin touch or touching infected lesions, barriers like gloves and gowns block the transfer of pathogens. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T6#GNS313_U1_T6_h3)

question: What is a fomite?

options.A: An inanimate object that can carry and transfer infectious germs
options.B: A living insect that transmits a parasite from animal to human
options.C: A specialized white blood cell that attacks invading bacteria
options.D: A type of protective mask worn during surgical procedures

explanation: Fomites are non-living items like door knobs, medical charts, and instruments that hold onto pathogens and pass them to new hosts. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T6#GNS313_U1_T6_h4)

question: Which scenario is a classic example of indirect contact transmission?

options.A: Getting infected with malaria from a mosquito bite during the rainy season
options.B: Catching a cold after touching a shared pen that an infected coworker used
options.C: Developing a wound infection from direct contact with a draining sore
options.D: Inhaling large respiratory droplets expelled by someone coughing nearby

explanation: The shared pen acts as a fomite, transferring the virus indirectly from the coworker's hand to the new host's hand. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T6#GNS313_U1_T6_h4)

question: How do airborne pathogens primarily travel to a new host?

options.A: Via large wet respiratory splashes falling straight to the floor
options.B: Through direct physical handshakes with infected individuals
options.C: By clinging to the legs of biting insects or household pets
options.D: As tiny dried droplet nuclei suspended in air currents

explanation: Airborne pathogens are so small and light that they float in the air for hours and travel long distances before being inhaled. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T6#GNS313_U1_T6_h5)

question: Why does a nurse need an N95 respirator instead of a standard surgical mask when caring for a patient with tuberculosis?

options.A: Airborne diseases can only be stopped if the nurse wears double face shields
options.B: Surgical masks are only designed to protect patients from the nurse's own breath
options.C: Tuberculosis is airborne, meaning tiny infectious particles float in the air and require tight filtration
options.D: Tuberculosis bacteria can easily dissolve through the thin material of a regular surgical mask

explanation: Standard surgical masks let tiny airborne particles slip through the sides, whereas N95 respirators seal tightly to filter out microscopic droplet nuclei. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T6#GNS313_U1_T6_h5)

question: What is a vector in the context of disease transmission?

options.A: A living organism, usually an insect, that carries a pathogen to a host
options.B: An open skin lesion that allows bacteria to enter the bloodstream
options.C: A drug resistant bacterial strain found in hospital wards
options.D: A contaminated hospital instrument used on multiple patients

explanation: Vectors are living carriers like mosquitoes, ticks, or fleas that transfer infectious agents from one animal or human to another. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T6#GNS313_U1_T6_h6)

question: What makes malaria an example of biological vector-borne transmission?

options.A: The mosquito only carries the parasite on the outside of its physical legs
options.B: The malaria parasite develops and multiplies inside the mosquito before being injected
options.C: The malaria pathogen is spread purely through human-to-human coughing
options.D: The disease can only live inside warm-blooded animal reservoirs

explanation: In biological transmission, the parasite undergoes a necessary part of its life cycle inside the vector before it can infect a new host. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T6#GNS313_U1_T6_h6)

question: Which of the following is considered a common vehicle for disease transmission?

options.A: Air currents in a closed hospital room
options.B: Direct skin-to-skin touch with a patient
options.C: A mosquito bite during the evening hours

explanation: Water, food, and blood are common vehicles capable of carrying pathogens to a large group of people simultaneously. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T6#GNS313_U1_T6_h7)

question: What is the main characteristic of a common vehicle outbreak?

options.A: Infection only spreads slowly from one family member to another over months
options.B: Pathogens travel exclusively through the air as dry microscopic dust
options.C: The disease can only be caught by direct physical contact in a hospital
options.D: Many people become infected simultaneously from a single contaminated source

explanation: Because a single food or water source serves many individuals, a common vehicle outbreak typically results in a sudden surge of cases. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T6#GNS313_U1_T6_h7)

question: What is recognized as the single most effective nursing action to prevent the spread of infections?

options.D: Placing all patients in isolation rooms

explanation: Handwashing and hand sanitizing remove transient microorganisms from the skin, preventing their transfer to patients. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T6#GNS313_U1_T6_h8)

question: A nurse cares for a patient with a drug-resistant wound infection. Which principle guides safe nursing care?

options.A: Treating all patient blood and body fluids as infectious using standard precautions
options.B: Reusing medical equipment between patients if it looks visually clean
options.C: Stopping all hand hygiene once gloves are removed from the hands
options.D: Assuming infection control is only necessary if the patient shows a high fever

explanation: Standard precautions require treating all bodily fluids as potentially infectious to protect against both known and unknown pathogens. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T6#GNS313_U1_T6_h8)
